learners.who: Mostly working professionals with three to ten years of experience. About half come from technical roles such as software development, IT support, or data analysis, and want to move into management. The rest come from business functions like finance, operations, or supply chain and have become the go-between for their department and IT. A smaller group are career changers and recent graduates, many of them international students drawn by the STEM designation. Most are in their first year of the program unless this is a capstone or elective.
learners.experience: The technical group already works with databases, code, and systems daily, but often hasn’t had to justify a technology decision in business terms. The business group knows budgets, processes, and stakeholders, and uses tools like Excel, ERP systems, or dashboards without knowing how they’re built. Common misconceptions to address: that technology projects fail for technical reasons (most fail on scope, people, or governance), that buying a system fixes a process, and that data quality is IT’s problem alone.
learners.motivation: They’re being asked to lead or sit in on technology decisions they don’t feel ready for. Typical problems include evaluating vendors, explaining a project’s value to leadership, managing a system rollout that users resist, and working with data they don’t trust. Many want a promotion or a move into roles like business analyst, IT manager, or product manager, and this course gives them language and frameworks they can use at work the next week.
learners.constraints: Full-time jobs, with most coursework happening in evenings and on weekends. Expect around 10 to 12 hours a week per course. Some travel for work, and international students or those on global teams may be in different time zones, which affects live cohort session timing. Technical background varies widely, so plan optional refreshers in SQL, spreadsheets, or business basics rather than assuming a shared starting point. Employer tuition support is common, which means some students need grades and completion on a fixed schedule.

description: Concepts regarding the design and use of computer-based management information and decision support systems; combinations of computing hardware and software and design concepts evaluated to meet managers' information needs. Classification 6 students may not enroll in this course.
plos:
1.	Apply programming fundamentals to write, debug, document, and integrate code, including handling exceptions and judging whether existing code libraries fit, so they can automate processes and solve business problems.
2.	Design and implement relational, NoSQL, and data warehouse solutions, including ETL processes, and justify the data storage architecture best suited to a business need based on performance, availability, and scale.
3.	Apply data mining, machine learning, optimization, and OLAP techniques to structured and unstructured data.
4.	Configure and automate secure cloud and network environments, and develop cloud adoption plans that address service selection, infrastructure management, and data security.
5.	Analyze cybersecurity threats, including human and social engineering factors, and risks to IT assets using ethical hacking tools and risk assessment methods; and design and evaluate technical, policy, cryptographic, and physical controls, incident response, and business continuity plans.
6.	Evaluate how IT initiatives and emerging technologies, including their ethical impact, align with business strategy, and develop project plans, portfolio priorities, and legacy modernization strategies that support digital transformation.
7.	Design user interfaces that account for users’ physical, cognitive, and emotional abilities, accessibility needs, and cultural context; devise usability tests to evaluate them; and justify design and technical decisions to non-technical stakeholders.
8.	Critically evaluate generative AI tools and automated platforms, and design their integration into business processes, system design, and software workflows to enhance productivity.
vision: Managers make better decisions when the right information reaches them in a form they can use. In this course, you’ll learn how management information and decision support systems are designed and used, and how to evaluate combinations of hardware, software, and design approaches against what managers actually need to know. You’ll practice turning vague requests from leaders into clear requirements and a technology recommendation you can defend. These skills prepare you to be the person leadership trusts when a major information decision is on the table.

clos.text: Evaluate a leader's ambiguous information request and translate it into a documented set of business requirements that justifies a recommended information system solution.

Analyze the scope, stakeholder, and governance risks that most often derail information system projects, and design a mitigation plan that addresses people and process factors alongside technical ones.
Evaluate competing technology or vendor options against business criteria such as cost, scalability, and strategic fit, and justify a recommendation to a non-technical executive audience.
Design a data governance approach that assigns data quality accountability across business and IT roles so that managers can trust the information driving their decisions.

assessments.title: Assignment: Vague Request Diagnosis
assessments.notes: Given a short vague request from a leader, students write a one-page memo naming the real information need behind the request and classifying it as a decision-support or transactional problem, with a brief rationale.
assessments.context: Mirrors the first move an analyst or new manager makes when an executive hands them an ambiguous ask with no clear system or solution attached.

assessments.title: Assignment: Requirements Translation Memo
assessments.notes: Given a one-paragraph request from a VP (e.g., 'our order data is a mess, fix it'), students write a 2-3 page requirements memo that lists functional and nonfunctional requirements, maps each to the business need it serves, and ends with a recommended solution direction (build, buy, or process fix) with a one-paragraph justification.
assessments.context: Mirrors the deliverable an analyst sends back to a VP after an intake conversation, before any vendor or build discussion starts.

assessments.title: Peerceptiv: Requirements Document Peer Review
assessments.notes: Students complete a calibration exercise on a sample requirements memo, then review two peers' Module 2 memos in Peerceptiv flagging specific gaps (ambiguous requirements, missing stakeholders, scope creep risks) and suggesting one concrete revision for each, followed by a short response to the feedback they received on their own memo.
assessments.context: Mirrors the stakeholder review cycle where colleagues critique a requirements document before it goes to leadership.

assessments.title: Assignment: Project Risk Mitigation Plan
assessments.notes: Given a short case describing a system rollout (e.g., an ERP implementation facing budget and timeline pressure), students build a risk register that identifies at least six scope, stakeholder, and governance risks, rates likelihood and impact, and writes a mitigation plan assigning an owner and specific action to each risk.
assessments.context: Mirrors a project manager preparing a risk register and mitigation plan for a steering committee before a system rollout begins.

assessments.title: Perusall: Vendor Selection Case Analysis
assessments.notes: Students annotate a case packet containing three competing vendor proposals, marking at least five annotations that evaluate each vendor against cost, scalability, and strategic fit, then reply to two classmates' annotations challenging or building on their reasoning before the live session.
assessments.context: Mirrors a procurement team reading vendor RFP responses side by side and flagging strengths, risks, and red flags before a decision meeting.

assessments.title: Assignment: Data Governance Charter
assessments.notes: Given two conflicting stakeholder accounts of a recurring data problem (e.g., a business lead blaming IT, an IT lead blaming unclear source entry), students write a governance charter that resolves the dispute by assigning clear data ownership and stewardship roles, defines at least three measurable data quality standards, and includes a one-paragraph rationale for why the accountability split will prevent the same conflict from recurring.
assessments.context: Mirrors drafting a data governance charter that assigns data quality accountability across business and IT roles.

assessments.title: Assignment: Business Case Narrative Draft
assessments.notes: Students submit a 2-3 page draft narrative that weaves their Module 4 risk findings and Module 5 vendor analysis into one coherent argument for a specific recommendation, with a short note on which pushback points they expect from leadership.
assessments.context: Mirrors the first full draft a manager writes before circulating a business case for internal review.

assessments.title: Assignment: Executive Pitch and Pushback Defense
assessments.notes: Students submit a slide deck summarizing their final recommendation (requirements, risks, vendor choice, governance plan) plus a recorded 8-10 minute presentation, and a written response to three anticipated executive pushback questions drawn from the Module 7 pushback notes.
assessments.context: Mirrors the live pitch and Q&A a manager faces when defending a technology investment to a leadership panel.
